title: Every Sport Suddenly Wants Another Champion
contentHtml:
Remember a few weeks ago, when I wrote about the impossible balancing act the PGA Tour was trying to strike in the evolution of its FedEx Cup playoff system?

“Put too much weight on the regular season, and the finale risks becoming a formality; put too little on it, and months of merit can be wiped away in a flash.”

Well, the Tour’s answer now seems be: Why balance them at all? Just crown two different champions.

Subscribe now

At least, that seems like one of the major takeaways from the big changes that the Tour announced this week would be forthcoming for the 2028 season — which also included the introduction of two separate tracks (the Championship Series and the Challenger Series) depending on a player’s status level, with promotion/relegation between the two levels, and the upper echelon’s championship culminating in a season-finale tournament that also doubles as a field-setter for a new two-week Tour Championship conducted via match play. The winner of that event will then be “a separate, standalone” Tour Champion.

Speaking with ESPN’s Mark Schlabach, PGA Tour boss Brian Rolapp — who was previously a high-ranking league executive at the NFL office — admitted the status quo wasn’t quite working. “I think one of the issues with the [current] Tour Championship was that I don’t think anyone really felt that it was culminating in crowning the best golfer in the world,” Rolapp said. “I feel like calling it the playoffs was almost doing it a disservice because it was just a separate competition.”

Now they have addressed that by splitting off the season-ending1 Tour Championship into its own separate-trophy side-quest, rather than incorporating it into the season-long championship format. And based on what I wrote a few weeks back, that’s probably a good thing. The history of the WGC Match Play tournament — perhaps a loose analogue2 for this new Tour Championship — was all over the place in terms of correlating seeds with success,3 but that may be a novel plus if this new winner is a “second champion” of sorts for the season.

More broadly, this move places golf squarely within the growing trend of sports and leagues attempting to inject side-championships into their traditional season structures — joining the WNBA (Commissioner’s Cup, announced 2019); NBA (NBA Cup, 2023); and NASCAR (In-Season Challenge, 2024).

The idealist side of me would argue that global soccer has had this model for a loooooong time — like, dating back to the 1800s — and that soccer in general takes a different approach to the very concept of each season’s “champion”, with teams usually vying for multiple different Cups in a given year. Some are more desirable and/or prestigious than others, but winning any of them warrants a celebration, and when the same team unifies all of them at the same time, it’s a particularly big deal. Overall, it’s another way to create meaning and stakes in a sport that’s supposed to be fun and entertaining.

Of course, the cynic in me would say that leagues are also suddenly doing this because it creates “new inventory” without actually having to do much extra work.

Think about it: A league already has games/races/tournaments on the calendar. They’re going to be played anyway. But by arbitrarily wrapping a bracket around some of them, assigning them a trophy and branding them as a “Cup” or “Challenge”, it automatically generates another product to sell to TV networks or streamers. They’re essentially making the same game count twice.

The PGA Tour sounds like it’s doing more than this — they’re genuinely restructuring the end of the schedule, for a number of reasons that go beyond made-for-TV cash-grabs4 — but the commercial logic remains hard to ignore.

At the same time, though, maybe these financial motives are also unwittingly leading these sports down a better path. (Let me explain…)
